query: Consider the following context: During the hot dip aluminum plating process, components such as sinking rollers, pulling rollers, and guide plates will come into long-term contact with high-temperature liquid aluminum and be corroded by the aluminum liquid, greatly reducing their service life. In that context, which material can be used for prepare parts for the dipping and plating equipment and protect the equipment from erosion, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using a refractory high‐entropy alloy, specifically an equiatomic Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy processed under conditions that promote a mixed BCC/HCP microstructure, will provide an effective erosion‐resistant barrier for parts (such as rollers and guide plates) in hot dip aluminum plating equipment.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 that is further processed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) to induce the formation of a dispersed HCP phase within a BCC matrix, increasing hardness.
generation.intervention: Replace or coat conventional materials with HIP-processed Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy components for parts that contact molten aluminum.
generation.conditions: Long-term exposure to high-temperature liquid aluminum (around or slightly above its melting point, e.g., ~700°C) during the hot dip aluminum plating process.
generation.structural_mediator: The HIP process-induced secondary HCP phase dispersed (more uniformly or at grain boundaries depending on processing) within the primary BCC matrix increases hardness and potentially forms a dense barrier that can inhibit aluminum penetration.
generation.mechanism: The increased microhardness and barrier effect from the mixed-phase microstructure reduce aluminum diffusion and mechanical erosion at the component surface, thereby protecting the underlying material from corrosion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components made from or coated with the HIP-processed Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy will exhibit lower erosion rates, reduced corrosion damage, and therefore an extended service life compared to standard materials currently in use.
generation.baseline: Standard dipping and plating equipment materials such as conventional tool steels or other alloys that currently experience rapid corrosion/erosion when exposed to molten aluminum.
generation.boundary: The protective effect is expected under controlled plating temperatures (~700°C) with exposure durations relevant to industrial processes; uncertainty remains regarding performance under cyclic thermal loads or prolonged exposure beyond typical operational times.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty about the alloy’s long-term oxidation behavior in a molten aluminum environment and whether the observed hardness improvements translate effectively into erosion resistance during cyclic thermal and mechanical stresses in actual service.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of test coupons: one set of HIP-processed Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy samples and one set of conventional material samples. Expose both sets to molten aluminum at a temperature representative of the hot dip plating process (around 700°C) for varying exposure times that simulate operational durations. Periodically remove samples to conduct weight loss measurements and microstructural analyses.
measurements: Surface and cross-sectional microstructural characterization (e.g., via SEM/EDS)
Hardness measurements before and after tests
Mechanical integrity tests under simulated service conditions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HIP-processed Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 alloy exhibits similar or greater weight loss, significant microstructural degradation (e.g., extensive aluminum penetration or phase instability), or reduced mechanical properties compared to the conventional materials, then the hypothesis that it provides improved erosion resistance would be falsified.

System: Ta20Nb20Hf20Zr20Ti20 (equiatomic atomic percentages). Processing: Vacuum arc melting (4 re-melts), casting into bars (gravity or suction-assisted), followed by Hot Isostatic Pressing (HIP) at 1230 °C and 152 MPa for 4 h. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile tests, compression tests at room temperature, and creep tests at 982 °C under 200 MPa and 120 MPa loads.
